title: It's really hot today
title_target: ဒီနေ့ အရမ်း ပူတယ် — dee-nay. a.yaⁿ: poo-dè
goal: Talking about the weather and the seasons — and grasping something that changes how you read all of Burmese: Burmese adjectives are really verbs.
bekal: using adjectives as full verbs with their endings
negating adjectives with မ … ဘူး
putting adjectives before nouns with …တဲ့

dialogs.title: စကားပြော — Waiting out the rain on the veranda
dialogs.intro: Ani and Mya Mya sit on the veranda at the start of the rainy season. Notice that every word that is an adjective in English — hot, cold, good, many — takes the ending တယ် here and is negated with မ … ဘူး, exactly like a verb.

lines.id: It's really hot today, isn't it?

grammars.title: ⚠️ Burmese adjectives are VERBS
body: This is the discovery that changes how you read all of Burmese, and it's best to grasp it now. ပူတယ် isn't "is" + "hot" but **"be-hot"** — one complete verb with its own ending. That's why it needs no word for "is", and it's negated with the frame မ … ဘူး you've known since unit 1.
after: The practical result is a big relief: **everything you've learned about verbs applies straight away to adjectives.** No new rules at all. ကောင်းပြီ means "it's good now"; မကောင်းသေးဘူး means "it's not good yet"; ကောင်းချင်တယ် means "want to be good".

⚠️ It also means that a sentence like "ဒီနေ့ ပူတယ်" **is already complete with nothing added**. Adding a verb "to be" such as ဖြစ်တယ် is actually wrong — a common mistake for beginners who think in English, where "is" is required.

grammars.title: Putting adjectives IN FRONT of nouns
body: When an adjective needs to describe a noun — "a cold season", "a good shop" — use the တဲ့ you learned in unit 13, and the whole thing stands **in front of** the noun.

head: English
Burmese
Say it
rows: အေးတဲ့ ရာသီ

after: There's also a short form with the prefix အ: အပူ (heat, as a noun), အအေး (cold), အကောင်း (goodness). You've already met it in the color names in unit 6 — အနီ, အပြာ — and in အလုပ် (work) from လုပ် (to work). The prefix အ turns a verb into a noun.

grammars.title: ပို and အ…ဆုံး — more and most
body: At A1, comparison needs only two tools: ပို (*poh*) for "more", and the wrap-around အ…ဆုံး for "most". Comparing two things is covered fully in unit 15.

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
rows: သိပ် မ…ဘူး

after: ⚠️ သိပ် (*thayk*) means "too" or "very", but in everyday use it **almost always comes with a negative**: သိပ်မအေးဘူး (not very cold). For "very" in a positive sentence, use အရမ်း (*a.yaⁿ:*).

grammars.title: Months and time spans
body: Month names are borrowed from English and end with လ (*la.*, "month"). For time spans, use ကနေ … အထိ ("from … until").

after: **ကနေ … အထိ** (*ga.-nay … a.htee.*) means "from … until/to" and works for both time and place: နိုဝင်ဘာကနေ ဖေဖော်ဝါရီအထိ (from November to February), ရန်ကုန်ကနေ မန္တလေးအထိ (from Yangon to Mandalay).

blocks.text: Unlike the four seasons of temperate countries or the two of much of the tropics, Myanmar divides its year into **three**. This isn't just weather talk — it sets when people plant, when monasteries take in novice monks, and when the big festivals are held.

blocks.title: ⚠️ သင်္ကြန် — a soaking-wet New Year
items: In mid-April, at the peak of the hot season, all of Myanmar stops work for almost a week for **သင်္ကြန်** (*thiⁿ-jaⁿ*), the Burmese New Year. The word comes from Sanskrit *saṃkrānti* — the same source as Songkran, the Thai New Year.

During သင်္ကြန်, people throw water at each other in the streets — a symbol of washing away the past year's misdeeds. Water stages line the main roads, and you **will** get wet if you leave the house, whatever you say.
Offices, banks, and many shops close. If you're planning a trip to Myanmar in April, check the dates first — travel can come to a complete halt for four days, and tickets sell out months ahead.
